name: Fluticasone
summary: Potent inhaled corticosteroid for maintenance control of asthma and COPD and for allergic rhinitis (intranasal), with very low oral bioavailability.
mechanism: Glucocorticoid receptor agonist that suppresses airway inflammation by down-regulating inflammatory cytokine and mediator production.

pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Inhaled: ~20–30% of delivered dose reaches the lungs; swallowed fraction <1% absorbed orally
pharmacokinetics.onset: Hours; maximal anti-inflammatory effect accumulates over days–weeks

dosing.adult: Asthma (HFA MDI): 88–440 mcg twice daily; nasal: 2 sprays per nostril once daily (furoate 27.5 mcg/spray)
dosing.maxDose: Asthma HFA: up to 880 mcg/day in severe disease

safety.pregnancy: Inhaled/intranasal — minimal systemic exposure; uncontrolled asthma is riskier than treatment
contraindications: Untreated systemic fungal or bacterial infection (systemic high-dose use)
warnings: Rinse mouth after inhaled use — oral candidiasis and dysphonia
Adrenal suppression with prolonged high doses
Reduced growth velocity in children — use the lowest effective dose
Increased pneumonia risk in COPD regimens containing an ICS
monitoring: Adrenal function with prolonged high-dose therapy
safety.overdose: Single-dose inhalation is unlikely to cause systemic effects; chronic high-dose use causes adrenal suppression

clinicalPearls: Fluticasone furoate (Avamys/Relvar) is more lipophilic and dosed once daily
Always rinse the mouth after inhaling to prevent candidiasis
good: First-line asthma controller with minimal systemic bioavailability
bad: Acute bronchospasm rescue; ICS monotherapy in COPD (combine with a LABA); strong CYP3A4 inhibitors raise systemic levels
